title: The Indo-European Languages
body: In 1786 William Jones observed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin must share a common origin. The insight founded historical linguistics. English belongs to the same family, as do most languages of Europe, Iran and northern India.

title: Runes
body: Runes were the alphabet of the early Germanic peoples. The Elder Futhark had 24 characters, while the Viking Age Younger Futhark had only 16. The Rök runestone in Sweden carries the longest known runic inscription.

title: The Origin of the Alphabet
body: Our Latin alphabet came via the Etruscans from the Greek alphabet, which was in turn adapted from the Phoenician script. The Greeks were the first to write vowels with their own letters.

title: Greek Building Blocks
body: Many English words are built from Greek parts, often coined long after antiquity. Democracy combines demos (people) and kratos (power); telephone combines tele (far) and phone (sound).

title: Ethos, Pathos and Logos
body: Aristotle described three ways to persuade: through the speaker's credibility (ethos), by stirring emotion (pathos) and with reasoned argument (logos). The distinction still underpins the teaching of rhetoric.

title: A Pyrrhic Victory
body: A Pyrrhic victory is a win so costly that it is almost a defeat. The phrase comes from King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who beat the Romans in 280–279 BC but lost so many men that he could not continue the war.

title: Norman French in English
body: After 1066 the ruling class in England spoke French for centuries. That is why English often has Germanic words for animals in the field (cow, pig, sheep) and French-derived words for the meat on the table (beef, pork, mutton).

title: Grimm's Law
body: Jacob Grimm described a regular sound shift that separated the Germanic languages from other Indo-European languages. It explains pairs such as Latin pater and English father, or Latin piscis and English fish.

title: The Rosetta Stone
body: Found in Egypt in 1799, the stone carries the same decree from 196 BC in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek. Because the Greek could be read, Jean-François Champollion was able to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

title: The Great Vowel Shift
body: Between roughly 1400 and 1700 the long vowels of English changed their pronunciation. Spelling had largely settled before the shift ended, which is a major reason English spelling and pronunciation often fail to match.

title: Crossing the Rubicon
body: In 49 BC Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon river into Italy, breaking Roman law and starting a civil war. To cross the Rubicon now means to take an irreversible step.

title: Salary and Salt
body: The word salary comes from the Latin salarium, which is related to sal, salt. The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is not well supported; the exact link between the word and salt remains uncertain.

title: Chinese Characters
body: Chinese is written with characters that mainly represent words or meaningful syllables rather than sounds alone. The earliest substantial examples are inscriptions on oracle bones from the Shang dynasty, more than 3,000 years ago, making it one of the oldest writing systems still in use.

title: Latin Abbreviations
body: Several everyday abbreviations come from Latin: e.g. (exempli gratia, for example), i.e. (id est, that is) and etc. (et cetera, and the rest). The two are often confused: e.g. introduces examples, while i.e. restates or narrows.

title: Pāṇini's Grammar
body: The Sanskrit grammarian Pāṇini, probably active around the 4th century BC, described the language in nearly 4,000 compact rules. His work is one of the earliest and most rigorous descriptions of any language and has influenced modern linguistics.

title: Prescriptive and Descriptive Grammar
body: Prescriptive grammar lays down how people ought to speak and write, as in rules against split infinitives or ending a sentence with a preposition. Descriptive grammar, the approach of modern linguistics, records how speakers actually use a language without judging it. Many familiar prescriptive rules were introduced by 18th- and 19th-century grammarians, some modelled on Latin, and linguists stress that non-standard dialects are as systematic as the standard.

title: Nebrija's Castilian Grammar
body: In 1492 Antonio de Nebrija published his Gramática de la lengua castellana, one of the first grammars of a modern European vernacular. In its dedication to Queen Isabella he wrote that language had always been the companion of empire. Appearing in the year of Columbus's first voyage, it came to symbolise the link between the Spanish language and Spain's expansion overseas.

title: The Septuagint
body: The Septuagint is the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. Its name, Latin for 'seventy', comes from the legend that seventy-two scholars produced it. It was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the early Church, the New Testament usually quotes it, and the Eastern Orthodox churches have used it as their Old Testament ever since.

title: Tone Languages
body: In a tone language the pitch of a syllable can change the meaning of a word. In Mandarin Chinese mā means mother and mǎ means horse; Cantonese, Vietnamese, Thai and Yoruba are also tonal. Tone languages are common in East and Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and parts of the Americas, and a large share of the world's languages use tone in some form.

title: Saussure and the Linguistic Sign
body: Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics, compiled by his students from lecture notes and published in 1916 after his death, laid the foundations of modern linguistics. He described the linguistic sign as a pairing of a sound-image (the signifier) and a concept (the signified), linked by convention rather than by nature. He also distinguished langue, the shared system, from parole, individual speech, and his ideas inspired structuralism across the humanities.

title: Kanji and Kana
body: Japanese is written with a mixture of scripts. Kanji, Chinese characters adopted by around the 5th century AD, write most nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives, while two syllabaries, hiragana and katakana, developed from simplified characters by around the 9th century. Hiragana writes grammatical endings and particles, and katakana is used mainly for foreign loanwords and emphasis.

title: The Austronesian Languages
body: Most linguists trace the Austronesian family to Taiwan, from where it spread through the Philippines and Indonesia and then across the Pacific and Indian Oceans over several thousand years. It includes Malay, Javanese, Tagalog, Malagasy in Madagascar, and the Polynesian languages of Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island. Before the colonial era it was among the most geographically widespread language families, a testament to the seafaring skills of its speakers.

title: The King James Bible
body: The English Bible commissioned by James I was published in 1611 after work by around fifty scholars. It drew heavily on William Tyndale's translation of the 1520s and 1530s, for which Tyndale had been executed as a heretic in 1536. Its phrasing, such as 'the salt of the earth' and 'a law unto themselves', passed into everyday English and shaped English prose for centuries.

title: The Navajo Code Talkers
body: During the Second World War the US Marine Corps recruited Navajo speakers to send messages in the Pacific in a code based on their language. Navajo was unwritten at the time for most purposes, grammatically complex and almost unknown outside the Navajo Nation, and the code was never broken by the Japanese. Their role remained classified until 1968, although many of them had been punished at school for speaking Navajo.

title: Brazil's Língua Geral
body: In colonial Brazil, Jesuit missionaries and settlers used a lingua franca based on Tupi, the língua geral, which in some regions was more widely spoken than Portuguese. In the 1750s the reforms of the Marquis of Pombal imposed Portuguese and restricted its use. A descendant, Nheengatu, is still spoken in the Amazon, and Tupi gave Portuguese and English words such as jaguar, piranha, tapioca and cashew.

title: Boycott
body: In 1880 Irish tenants, organised by the Land League in a campaign against high rents and evictions, refused all dealings with Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent in County Mayo. Labourers would not work his fields and shops would not serve him. His name quickly became a word for collective refusal to deal with a person, firm or country, a tactic later used from the Indian independence movement to the campaign against apartheid.

title: The Bantu Expansion
body: The Bantu languages, a branch of the Niger–Congo family, are spoken across most of Africa south of the equator, from Kikongo and Swahili to Zulu and Shona. Their close similarities reflect a spread of farming peoples from the region of today's Nigeria and Cameroon that began several thousand years ago. Bantu languages typically sort nouns into many classes marked by prefixes, as in Swahili mtu (person) and watu (people).

title: Dhvani: Suggestion in Sanskrit Poetics
body: The Kashmiri critic Anandavardhana argued in the 9th century that the soul of poetry is dhvani, 'suggestion': meaning that is neither stated nor logically implied but evoked. A poem may describe only a scene, for example, yet convey longing. His theory, developed by Abhinavagupta, became central to Sanskrit poetics and anticipates modern ideas about implied meaning and connotation.

title: The Turkic Languages
body: The Turkic languages, including Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur, Tatar and Yakut, stretch from the Balkans to north-eastern Siberia. Their earliest substantial texts are the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions in Mongolia, carved in an Old Turkic script that resembles runes. Some scholars group Turkic with Mongolic and Tungusic in an 'Altaic' family, but most linguists now attribute their similarities to long contact rather than common descent.

title: The Indo-European Homeland Debate
body: Where Proto-Indo-European was spoken has long been debated. The steppe (or Kurgan) hypothesis places it north of the Black and Caspian Seas around 4000–3000 BC, while the Anatolian hypothesis links its spread to early farmers moving out of Anatolia. Ancient DNA studies published from 2015 onwards found large population movements from the steppe into Europe around 3000 BC, which many scholars see as strong support for the steppe view.

title: Arabic Words in European Languages
body: Medieval contact through Spain, Sicily and the Mediterranean brought many Arabic words into European languages. Algebra comes from al-jabr in the title of a book by al-Khwarizmi, whose own name gave algorithm; zero and cipher come from Arabic sifr, itself a translation of Sanskrit śūnya, 'empty'. Admiral, alchemy, alcohol, sugar and tariff also reached English through Arabic.

title: The Māori Language Revival
body: By the 1970s te reo Māori was spoken by a shrinking and ageing population after decades in which schools had discouraged it. Activists responded: a petition in 1972 led to an annual Māori Language Day, and from 1982 kōhanga reo, 'language nests', immersed preschool children in Māori. The Māori Language Act 1987 made it an official language of New Zealand, and the revival has inspired indigenous language movements elsewhere.

title: Yan Fu's Three Principles of Translation
body: Yan Fu introduced Western ideas to China through translations of works such as Thomas Huxley's Evolution and Ethics, published in the late 1890s, and Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations. In his preface to the Huxley translation he set out three criteria for a good translation: faithfulness (xin), expressiveness (da) and elegance (ya). The formula became a touchstone of translation theory in China.

title: Coptic
body: Coptic is the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language, written from the early centuries AD in the Greek alphabet with several extra letters taken from Demotic. It was the language of Christian Egypt until Arabic gradually replaced it after the Arab conquest, and it survives as the liturgical language of the Coptic Church. Champollion's knowledge of Coptic was crucial to his decipherment of hieroglyphs.

title: Tocharian
body: In the early 20th century, expeditions to the Tarim Basin in what is now western China found manuscripts from roughly the 6th to 8th centuries AD in two previously unknown languages, now called Tocharian A and B. Written in a Brahmi-derived script and largely containing Buddhist texts, they proved to be Indo-European. Their location, far to the east of any other ancient Indo-European language, changed ideas about the family's early spread.

title: Orwell's Politics and the English Language
body: In his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', George Orwell argued that vague, inflated prose helps to hide ugly realities, as when bombing defenceless villages is called 'pacification'. He offered six rules, including never using a long word where a short one will do. The essay is widely cited on clear writing and political euphemism, themes he developed in Nineteen Eighty-Four.

title: Haitian Creole
body: Haitian Creole emerged among enslaved Africans on the plantations of French Saint-Domingue, with a vocabulary mostly from French but a grammar very different from it; creolists debate how much it owes to West African languages. It is the first language of nearly all Haitians, while French long remained the language of the elite and the state. The 1987 constitution made Creole an official language alongside French.

title: The Revival of Hebrew
body: For about two thousand years Hebrew was used mainly for prayer and scholarship rather than everyday speech. From the 1880s Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who settled in Jerusalem, championed it as a spoken language, raised his son in Hebrew and compiled a dictionary of modern Hebrew. Schools in the Jewish settlements adopted it, and it became an official language of Israel; it is the best-known case of a language revived for daily use.

title: Isolating, Agglutinative and Fusional Languages
body: Linguists classify languages by how they build words. Isolating languages such as Vietnamese use mostly invariable words; agglutinative languages such as Turkish and Finnish string together suffixes that each carry one meaning; fusional languages such as Latin pack several meanings, like case and number, into a single ending. Polysynthetic languages, found especially in the Arctic and the Americas, can express a whole sentence in one long word.

title: The Indus Script
body: The Indus or Harappan civilisation of around 2600–1900 BC left thousands of short inscriptions, mostly on stamp seals, using several hundred signs. The script remains undeciphered: the inscriptions are very short, no bilingual text has been found, and the language behind them is unknown. Scholars even debate whether the signs fully encoded language.

title: Webster's American Dictionary
body: Noah Webster published his American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828, aiming to give the United States a linguistic identity of its own. He promoted spellings such as color, center and defense, which became the American standard. Earlier, his 'blue-backed speller', first published in 1783, had taught generations of American children to read.

title: Metaphor and Metonymy
body: A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another ('time is money'), while metonymy refers to something by an associated thing, as when 'the Crown' stands for the monarchy. Both were classified as figures of speech by ancient rhetoricians. Since George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By (1980), many linguists have argued that metaphor structures everyday thought, not just poetry.

title: Yiddish
body: Yiddish developed among Ashkenazi Jews, probably in the Rhineland, roughly a thousand years ago, combining a German base with Hebrew and Aramaic words and, after migration eastwards, Slavic elements. It is written in the Hebrew alphabet. Before the Holocaust it was spoken by millions across Central and Eastern Europe and had a rich modern literature, recognised when Isaac Bashevis Singer won the Nobel Prize in 1978.

title: Indonesian as a National Language
body: At the Youth Pledge of 28 October 1928, nationalists in the Dutch East Indies vowed to uphold 'the language of unity, Indonesian'. They chose a form of Malay, long a trading lingua franca of the archipelago, rather than Javanese, the language of the largest ethnic group. As the official language of independent Indonesia, it became a shared language across hundreds of ethnic groups and is often cited as a model of successful language planning.

title: The Shuowen Jiezi
body: Compiled by the scholar Xu Shen around AD 100, the Shuowen Jiezi was the first Chinese dictionary to analyse the structure of characters. It arranged about 9,000 characters under 540 radicals, or shared components, and explained each one's meaning and composition. Its radical system shaped later Chinese dictionaries, and its analyses remain important for the history of the script.

title: Tamazight and Tifinagh
body: The Berber, or Amazigh, languages have been spoken in North Africa since long before the Arab conquests but long lacked official status. Morocco made Tamazight an official language in its 2011 constitution, and Algeria did the same in 2016. Morocco adopted a modern form of the ancient Tifinagh script, which had survived among the Tuareg, for teaching the language in schools.

title: The Académie Française
body: Founded in 1635 under Cardinal Richelieu, the Académie française was charged with regulating the French language and producing an authoritative dictionary, the first edition of which appeared in 1694. Its forty members, known as 'the immortals', are elected for life. It became a model for language academies elsewhere, such as the Real Academia Española, founded in 1713.

title: The Bengali Language Movement
body: When Pakistan was created in 1947, its eastern wing, today's Bangladesh, spoke mainly Bengali, but the government sought to make Urdu the sole national language. On 21 February 1952 police fired on protesting students in Dhaka, killing several. The movement won recognition for Bengali, fed the nationalism that led to Bangladesh's independence in 1971, and UNESCO later made 21 February International Mother Language Day.

title: Mandarin and Standard Chinese
body: The English word mandarin came via Portuguese from Malay, ultimately from Sanskrit mantrin, 'adviser', and first meant an imperial Chinese official. The officials' common language, guanhua, was based on northern speech and served as a lingua franca across the empire. In the 20th century a standard based on Beijing pronunciation became the national language, while other Chinese varieties such as Cantonese and Hokkien are not mutually intelligible with it.

title: Linear B
body: Linear B is a script found on clay tablets from Mycenaean Greece and Crete in the second half of the second millennium BC. In 1952 the architect Michael Ventris, later working with John Chadwick, showed that it recorded an early form of Greek, centuries older than Homer. The tablets are mostly palace administrative records, and the related Linear A script of Minoan Crete remains undeciphered.

title: Rongorongo
body: Rongorongo is a system of glyphs carved on a few dozen wooden objects from Easter Island (Rapa Nui), first reported by outsiders in the 1860s. It has never been deciphered, and scholars disagree on whether it is true writing and whether it arose before or after contact with Europeans in the 18th century. If it is writing invented on the island without outside influence, it would be one of the very few independent inventions of writing.

title: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement
body: From the late 8th to the 10th century, scholars in Abbasid Baghdad translated a large part of Greek philosophy, medicine and science into Arabic, often via Syriac. Patrons included the caliph al-Ma'mun, and the Nestorian Christian Hunayn ibn Ishaq was among the most prolific translators. The movement preserved and extended the works of Aristotle, Galen and Euclid, many of which later reached medieval Europe through Arabic.

title: The Afroasiatic Languages
body: The Afroasiatic family includes Arabic, Hebrew and Aramaic, the Berber languages, Hausa, Somali and Amharic, as well as ancient Egyptian and Akkadian. It probably originated in north-eastern Africa, though its homeland is debated. Its Semitic branch builds words from roots of usually three consonants: in Arabic, k-t-b gives kataba (he wrote), kitab (book) and maktab (office).

title: Quechua
body: Quechua served as the administrative language of the Inca Empire, which spread it along the Andes. After the Spanish conquest, missionaries adopted it as a 'general language' for evangelisation, extending it further, and a catechism printed in Lima in 1584 in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara was the first book printed in South America. Quechua is in fact a family of related varieties spoken across several Andean countries.

title: Basic Word Order
body: Languages differ in the usual order of subject, verb and object. English, Chinese and Swahili are mainly subject-verb-object; Japanese, Korean, Turkish and Hindi put the verb last; Classical Arabic, Welsh and Irish usually put it first. Joseph Greenberg showed in the 1960s that word order correlates with other features: verb-final languages, for example, tend to use postpositions rather than prepositions.

title: Sequoyah's Cherokee Syllabary
body: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who could not read any language, devised a writing system for Cherokee and completed it around 1821. Each of its characters stands for a syllable. The Cherokee Nation adopted it, literacy spread rapidly, and the newspaper Cherokee Phoenix began printing in it in 1828. It is a rare case of an individual creating a successful script without being literate beforehand.

title: Nicaraguan Sign Language
body: When Nicaragua opened schools for deaf children in the late 1970s and 1980s, pupils who had used only home signs began to create a shared signing system, and younger children who joined later turned it into a fuller language with consistent grammar. Linguists studied it as a rare chance to watch a language being born. It confirmed what research since William Stokoe's 1960 work on American Sign Language had shown: sign languages are complete natural languages.

title: Writing the Hawaiian Language
body: American Protestant missionaries who arrived in Hawaii in 1820 worked with Hawaiian speakers to put the language into writing, settling by the late 1820s on an alphabet of only twelve letters: five vowels and seven consonants. Schools and printing spread literacy remarkably quickly, and Hawaiian-language newspapers flourished from the 1830s onwards. After an 1896 law made English the medium of schooling, the language declined sharply, and much of this printed record later became a key resource for its revival.

title: Swahili
body: Swahili developed on the East African coast as the Bantu language of trading towns in contact with Arabia, Persia and India, and it absorbed many Arabic words; its name comes from Arabic sawahil, 'coasts'. It was long written in Arabic script before the Latin alphabet took over in the colonial era. It spread inland as a lingua franca of East Africa and became a symbol of national unity in Tanzania after independence.

title: The Uralic Languages
body: Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian are not Indo-European but belong to the Uralic family, named after the Ural Mountains, near which it probably originated. The family also includes the Sámi languages of northern Scandinavia and many smaller languages of Russia. Uralic languages typically add chains of suffixes to words, and many have large case systems and vowel harmony.

title: The Armenian Alphabet
body: Around AD 405 the monk Mesrop Mashtots created an alphabet for Armenian, which had previously been written, if at all, in foreign scripts. Its first major use was a translation of the Bible, and a rich literature followed, including translations of Greek works that are now lost in the original. The alphabet has been used for Armenian ever since, and Mashtots is venerated as a saint by the Armenian Church.

title: A Language Is a Dialect with an Army
body: The line between a language and a dialect is often political rather than linguistic. The Yiddish scholar Max Weinreich popularised the quip that 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy' in the 1940s. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish are largely mutually intelligible yet count as separate languages, while some Chinese varieties called dialects are not mutually intelligible at all.

title: Sanskrit
body: Sanskrit, the classical language of ancient India, is an Indo-European language whose oldest form appears in the Rigveda, composed perhaps around 1500–1200 BC and long transmitted orally. Its classical form became the language of Hindu scripture, philosophy, science and court poetry, and was also used by Buddhists and Jains. For over a thousand years it served as a prestige language of learning and kingship across South and Southeast Asia.

title: Basque, a Language Isolate
body: Basque, spoken in the western Pyrenees of Spain and France, is a language isolate: it has no demonstrated relationship with any other living language. It was spoken in the region before the Indo-European languages arrived and survived Roman rule and centuries of pressure from Latin, Spanish and French. Its grammar is ergative, marking the subject of a transitive verb differently from the subject of an intransitive one.

title: Cuneiform
body: Cuneiform, meaning 'wedge-shaped', was developed in Sumer around 3200 BC, first for keeping accounts, and was written by pressing a reed stylus into clay. Over three millennia it was adapted for many languages, including Akkadian, Hittite and Old Persian, before dying out around the 1st century AD. Its decipherment in the 19th century relied heavily on Henry Rawlinson's copies of the trilingual Behistun inscription in Iran.

title: The Mongolian Script
body: The traditional Mongolian script, written in vertical columns, was adopted under Genghis Khan in the early 13th century from the Old Uyghur alphabet. That alphabet came from the script of the Sogdians, Iranian merchants who were key middlemen of the Silk Road, and ultimately from Aramaic. Mongolia switched to Cyrillic in the 1940s, while the vertical script continued in use in Inner Mongolia in China.

title: Grice's Maxims of Conversation
body: The philosopher Paul Grice argued, in lectures from the late 1960s, that conversation rests on a cooperative principle: speakers are expected to be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. When a speaker seems to break one of these maxims, listeners infer an unstated meaning, which Grice called an implicature. A reference letter praising only a candidate's handwriting, for example, implies a weak candidate.

title: Hangul
body: Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was created at the court of King Sejong and promulgated in 1446 in a text called Hunminjeongeum, 'the correct sounds for instructing the people'. Until then Koreans wrote in Classical Chinese, which few could master. Its consonant shapes were designed to depict the speech organs, and its letters are grouped into syllable blocks; South Korea celebrates its creation each October on Hangul Day.

title: Brahmi and Its Descendant Scripts
body: The Brahmi script is first securely attested in the edicts of the emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BC, and James Prinsep deciphered it in the 1830s. It is an abugida: each consonant carries an inherent vowel, which is changed by added marks. Brahmi is the ancestor of Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil and other Indian scripts, and also of the Tibetan, Thai, Burmese, Khmer and Javanese scripts.

title: Vietnamese Quốc Ngữ
body: Quốc ngữ, the Latin-based alphabet of Vietnamese, was developed in the 17th century by Portuguese and other Catholic missionaries, and Alexandre de Rhodes's dictionary of 1651 helped fix it. Diacritics mark Vietnamese tones and vowel qualities. Promoted under French rule and then by Vietnamese nationalists as a route to mass literacy, it replaced Classical Chinese and the character-based chữ Nôm in the early 20th century.

title: Classical Chinese Across East Asia
body: For many centuries Classical Chinese was the shared written language of East Asia, used by scholars and officials in Korea, Japan and Vietnam much as Latin was used in Europe. Each country read the texts with its own pronunciation, and huge numbers of Chinese-derived words entered Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese. As a result, a large part of the vocabulary of these unrelated languages is of Chinese origin.

title: The Oxford English Dictionary
body: The Oxford English Dictionary began in 1857 when the Philological Society called for a new dictionary recording the history of English words. Under its chief editor James Murray it appeared in instalments from 1884 and was completed in 1928. Built on millions of quotation slips sent in by volunteer readers, it traces each word's meanings in the order of their first recorded use.

title: The Invention of Writing
body: Writing was invented independently at least three times: in Mesopotamia around 3200 BC, in China by about 1200 BC and in Mesoamerica in the first millennium BC. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at about the same time as Mesopotamian cuneiform, and scholars debate whether they arose independently. A key step was the rebus principle, using a sign for its sound rather than its meaning, which let scribes write names and grammatical words.

title: The Inca Khipu
body: Without a conventional script, the Incas kept records on khipus, cords of cotton or camelid fibre with knots tied in a decimal system. Specialists called khipukamayuq used them for censuses, tribute and accounts, and Spanish officials sometimes accepted their readings as evidence. Whether some khipus also recorded narratives or language, and not only numbers, is still debated.

title: Dara Shikoh's Persian Upanishads
body: In 1657 the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh, eldest son of Shah Jahan, had some fifty Upanishads translated from Sanskrit into Persian, believing they shared truths with the Quran. The French scholar Anquetil-Duperron translated this Persian version into Latin in the early 1800s. Through it the Upanishads reached European readers such as Schopenhauer, who called them the consolation of his life.

title: Turkey's 1928 Alphabet Reform
body: In 1928 Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's government replaced the Arabic script, used for Ottoman Turkish for centuries, with a Latin-based alphabet adapted to Turkish sounds. The change was enforced within months, and Atatürk himself toured the country teaching the new letters. A language reform followed that replaced many Arabic and Persian loanwords with Turkish ones, making Ottoman texts hard for later generations to read.

title: Meiji Japan's New Vocabulary
body: As Meiji Japan absorbed Western learning in the late 19th century, scholars coined many words from Chinese characters for new concepts. Nishi Amane is credited with tetsugaku (philosophy), and terms such as keizai (economy) and shakai (society) took on their modern meanings in this period. Many of these coinages were then borrowed into Chinese and Korean, so much modern East Asian intellectual vocabulary was shaped in Japan.

title: Nahuatl
body: Nahuatl was the language of the Aztecs and a lingua franca of central Mexico before the Spanish conquest. Spanish friars wrote grammars of it in Latin letters, and works such as Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex recorded Aztec culture in Nahuatl and Spanish. Through Spanish it gave English words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli, and it is spoken in Mexico to this day.

title: Sibawayh and the Founding of Arabic Grammar
body: Sibawayh, a Persian scholar working in Basra in the late 8th century, wrote the first comprehensive grammar of Arabic, known simply as al-Kitab, 'the Book'. His teacher al-Khalil ibn Ahmad compiled the first Arabic dictionary, Kitab al-Ayn, and systematised the metres of Arabic poetry. Their work, driven partly by concern for the correct reading of the Quran, founded the Arabic linguistic tradition.

title: Jerome's Vulgate
body: In the late 4th century Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome to revise the Latin Bible. Working largely in Bethlehem, Jerome translated most of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than from the Greek Septuagint. His version, later called the Vulgate (the 'common' edition), became the standard Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years, and the Council of Trent declared it authoritative in 1546.

title: Australian Aboriginal Languages
body: At the time of British colonisation Australia had around 250 languages, most belonging to the Pama-Nyungan family, and many have since died out or have few speakers. Some show striking features: Guugu Yimithirr describes positions using compass directions rather than left and right. The same language gave English the word kangaroo, recorded by James Cook's expedition in 1770.

title: Baybayin
body: Baybayin is a pre-colonial script of the Philippines, an abugida related to the Brahmi-derived scripts of Indonesia. Spanish observers in the 16th century noted its wide use for Tagalog, and the Doctrina Christiana of 1593, among the first books printed in the Philippines, used it alongside Latin letters. It gave way to the Latin alphabet under Spanish rule but has become a symbol of Filipino heritage.

title: From Latin to the Romance Languages
body: Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian descend not from classical literary Latin but from the spoken Latin of ordinary people, often called Vulgar Latin. After the Western Roman Empire fragmented, regional speech drifted apart until it was recognised as distinct from Latin. The Strasbourg Oaths of 842 are often cited as the earliest text in an early form of French.

title: The Phoneme
body: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another in a particular language. In English, p and b are separate phonemes because they separate pin from bin, but sounds that are distinct in one language may count as one in another: Japanese, for instance, does not distinguish English r and l. The concept is the foundation of phonology and of alphabetic spelling.

title: The Sapir–Whorf Hypothesis
body: The idea that the language we speak shapes how we think is linked to the American linguist Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, writing between the 1920s and 1940s. Its strong form, that language determines thought, is now generally rejected. Experiments have, however, found weaker effects, for instance on how speakers of different languages divide up colours or describe directions.

title: Click Consonants
body: Click consonants, made by drawing the tongue sharply away from the roof of the mouth, are ordinary speech sounds almost only in southern and eastern Africa. They are characteristic of the languages often grouped as Khoisan, spoken by San and Khoekhoe peoples, and were borrowed into neighbouring Bantu languages such as Zulu and Xhosa. In writing, the letters c, q and x often represent clicks, as at the start of the name Xhosa.

title: Esperanto
body: Esperanto was published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor from Białystok in the Russian Empire, under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'. He designed it as an easy, neutral second language with regular grammar and vocabulary drawn mainly from European languages. Unlike most invented languages, it gained a lasting international community of speakers, including some who learned it from birth.

title: Tamil and the Dravidian Languages
body: Tamil belongs to the Dravidian family, which also includes Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam and is unrelated to the Indo-European languages of northern India. Tamil has a continuous literary tradition reaching back about two thousand years to the Sangam poetry, and its early grammar, the Tolkappiyam, is of uncertain but early date. In 2004 the Indian government declared Tamil the first 'classical language' of India.

title: Persian, a Language of Empires
body: After the Arab conquest of Iran, New Persian emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries, written in Arabic script with many Arabic loanwords, and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh helped establish it as a literary language. For centuries Persian was a language of administration, poetry and diplomacy from Anatolia to Central Asia and India, including at the Mughal court. Its influence shows in the vocabulary of Turkish, Urdu, Hindi and many other languages.

title: The International Phonetic Alphabet
body: The International Phonetic Alphabet was created by the International Phonetic Association, founded in Paris in 1886, to give one symbol to each distinct speech sound in any language. Based largely on Latin letters with additions such as ʃ and ŋ, it lets linguists, language teachers and dictionaries record pronunciation unambiguously. It has been revised periodically as knowledge of the world's sounds has grown.

title: The Vernacular Chinese Movement
body: For two thousand years formal Chinese writing used Classical Chinese, a terse literary language far from everyday speech. Around 1917 reformers such as Hu Shi and Chen Duxiu called for writing in the vernacular, baihua, and Lu Xun's story 'A Madman's Diary' (1918) showed what modern fiction in it could do. Linked to the May Fourth Movement, the change brought written Chinese close to spoken Mandarin.

title: The Maya Script
body: The Maya of Mesoamerica wrote with several hundred glyphs combining word signs and syllable signs, carving texts on monuments and painting them in bark-paper books, of which only a handful survive. For a long time scholars believed the script recorded mainly calendars and astronomy. From the 1950s, building on the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov's phonetic approach, researchers deciphered most of it, revealing the histories of kings and city-states.

title: Aramaic
body: Aramaic spread across the Near East as a language of trade and administration under the Assyrian and then the Persian Achaemenid empires. It replaced Hebrew as the everyday language of many Jews, parts of the Bible and the Talmud are written in it, and Jesus is generally thought to have spoken it. Its alphabet gave rise to the square Hebrew script and, through Nabataean and Syriac, to the Arabic script and others across Asia.

title: Language Endangerment
body: Several thousand languages are spoken in the world, but many have few speakers and are no longer learned by children. When a community shifts to a dominant language, its own can vanish within a few generations, as Manx did as a native language when its last native speaker died in 1974. The United Nations declared 2019 the International Year of Indigenous Languages and 2022–2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.

title: The Five Canons of Rhetoric
body: Classical rhetoric divided the art of speaking into five parts, set out in Roman handbooks such as the Rhetorica ad Herennium and in Cicero's writings: invention (finding arguments), arrangement, style, memory and delivery. Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria, written in the 1st century AD, built a whole education around this scheme. It shaped European schooling from antiquity into modern times.

title: Kashgari's Compendium of Turkic Dialects
body: In the 1070s Mahmud al-Kashgari, a Turkic scholar from Kashgar, wrote the Diwan Lughat al-Turk in Baghdad to teach Arabic speakers the languages of the Turks. It explains Turkic words in Arabic, records dialects, proverbs and poetry, and includes a round map of the Turkic world. It is a foundational source for the history of the Turkic languages and peoples.

title: Arabic Diglossia
body: Arabic speakers use two varieties side by side. Modern Standard Arabic, descended from the Classical Arabic of the Quran, is used in writing, news and formal speech across the Arab world, while everyday life is conducted in regional dialects, such as Egyptian or Moroccan Arabic, which can differ greatly. The linguist Charles Ferguson named such splits diglossia in 1959, comparing Arabic with Greek, Swiss German and Haitian Creole.

title: Braille
body: Louis Braille, blinded in a childhood accident, developed his reading system as a teenager at the Paris institute for blind youth and published it in 1829. Each character is formed from a cell of up to six raised dots that can be read by touch. Adapted to many languages and to music and mathematics, braille gave blind people practical access to reading and writing.

title: N'Ko
body: In 1949 the Guinean scholar Solomana Kanté created the N'Ko alphabet for the Manding languages of West Africa, such as Maninka and Bambara; n'ko means 'I say' in all of them. He reportedly wanted to answer claims that African languages could not be properly written. Written from right to left and marking tones, N'Ko has been used for a substantial literature and promoted as a tool of education and cultural self-confidence.

title: Kumarajiva's Buddhist Translations
body: Kumarajiva, a monk from the Silk Road kingdom of Kucha, was brought to Chang'an in 401 and led a large translation bureau there until his death. His fluent Chinese versions of texts such as the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra became the standard ones read in East Asian Buddhism. The translation of Buddhist scriptures, continued later by Xuanzang, enriched Chinese with many new words and concepts.

title: The Cyrillic Alphabet
body: In the 860s the Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius were sent to evangelise the Slavs of Great Moravia and created the Glagolitic alphabet for Old Church Slavonic. Their followers in the First Bulgarian Empire soon developed Cyrillic, based largely on Greek letters, and named it in Cyril's honour. Cyrillic spread with Orthodox Christianity and is used for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and other languages.

title: Hindi and Urdu
body: Hindi and Urdu share a common spoken base, often called Hindustani, that grew up around Delhi from the late medieval period. Urdu is written in a Perso-Arabic script and draws its learned vocabulary from Persian and Arabic, while standard Hindi is written in Devanagari and draws on Sanskrit. The split hardened in the 19th century amid religious and political rivalry, and after 1947 Hindi became an official language of India and Urdu the national language of Pakistan.

title: Tok Pisin
body: Tok Pisin, 'talk pidgin', grew from an English-based pidgin used on plantations in the 19th century and became the main lingua franca of Papua New Guinea, a country with hundreds of indigenous languages. A pidgin is a simplified contact language; when children grow up speaking it as a first language it becomes a creole with a full grammar. Tok Pisin has become an official language of the country and the mother tongue of many town dwellers.

title: Luther's German Bible
body: Martin Luther translated the New Testament into German in 1522, working from Erasmus's Greek edition, and published the complete Bible in 1534. He aimed to write as ordinary people spoke, listening, as he put it, to the mother in the home and the common man in the market. Printed in vast numbers, his translation helped spread a common written standard across the German-speaking lands and shaped modern German.

title: Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education
body: In 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay, a member of the governor-general's council, argued that British India should fund education in English rather than in Sanskrit and Arabic, dismissing Indian learning in notoriously contemptuous terms. He aimed to create a class of Indians 'English in taste' to act as intermediaries. English became the language of higher education and administration, and it continued as an official language after independence.

title: Ge'ez and the Ethiopic Script
body: Ge'ez was the language of the kingdom of Aksum in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, and its script developed from South Arabian writing. By around the 4th century AD vowel marks were attached to the consonants, turning it into an abugida. Ge'ez has remained the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and its script is used for Amharic and Tigrinya.

title: Evidentiality
body: Some languages require speakers to mark how they know what they report. In Turkish, different past-tense suffixes distinguish events the speaker witnessed from things heard about or inferred, and Quechua uses markers for direct knowledge, hearsay and conjecture. This grammatical category, called evidentiality, shows that languages differ not only in what they can say but in what they oblige speakers to say.

title: Chomsky and Universal Grammar
body: In Syntactic Structures (1957) Noam Chomsky proposed describing a language as a system of rules that generate all and only its grammatical sentences. He argued that children acquire language so quickly from limited input that humans must have an innate capacity for it, a universal grammar. His ideas transformed linguistics and cognitive science, though how much of grammar is innate remains debated.

title: Johnson's Dictionary
body: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language, published in 1755, was compiled by Johnson with a few assistants over about nine years. It defined more than 40,000 words and illustrated their meanings with more than 100,000 quotations from English writers, a method later adopted by the Oxford English Dictionary. It remained the leading English dictionary for more than a century.

title: Chinese Script Reform in the 1950s
body: In the 1950s the People's Republic of China launched two reforms intended to raise literacy. Simplified characters, with fewer strokes, replaced many traditional forms in mainland China, while Taiwan and Hong Kong kept the traditional ones. Hanyu Pinyin, adopted in 1958, spells Mandarin in Latin letters with tone marks and is used to teach pronunciation and to type characters.
